entry.title: The Result pattern has a hole, and it's where your bugs hide
entry.summary:
Errors-as-values is one of the better ideas to reach mainstream TypeScript. Instead of throwing an exception that the type system can't see, a function returns a Result<T, E> and failure becomes part of the type. neverthrow, boxed, byethrow, and effect all give you some version of it, and if you've adopted one you already know why it's worth it. But most of them stop one step short, and that step is where a specific class of bug lives: the kind that looks like a domain error but isn't. This post is about that gap, why it matters, and how a small library called unthrown closes it. A thrown exception is invisible to the type system. Consider: function fetchUser(id: string): User
It promises a User. It says nothing about the NotFoundError, the TimeoutError, or the TypeError from a typo three…

entry.title: Understanding Shannon entropy: A brief into quantifying Information
entry.summary:
How randomness became one of the simplest signals in modern data security. When we hear the word entropy, most of us think of thermodynamics. Surprisingly, the same mathematical concept quietly powers many security systems used by modern software companies. It isn't used to encrypt data and neither identify secrets with absolute certainty. Instead, it answers a much simpler and computationally inexpensive question: Does this string look unusually random? That single question turns out to be incredibly useful when scanning millions of log entries, chat messages, API payloads, and source code files. What exactly is Shannon entropy?

entry.summary: Originally published on tamiz.pro. entry.summary: Somewhere around the third feature request in a row, I noticed I was burning a full Claude Code session on work that did not need it. Adding a pagination parameter to an endpoint.
